headline: High-risk shared filesystem and shell overlap create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystems and execute shell commands, so a shared workspace can carry attacker-controlled content from agent_a into agent_b or vice versa. agent_a explicitly shares state via filesystem and git only, while agent_b writes files in a local development environment. No direct provenance or isolation is documented, so the interaction is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b operate on the same working directory or git checkout, prompt injection is possible through files.
IF agent_b ingests repository or notebook content as instructions, attacker-controlled text can steer behavior.
mitigations: Use separate directories for the two agents.
Disable automatic execution of file contents as instructions.
Review any files passed between agents before reuse.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: isolate agents with separate containers or users.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches source code, git history, shell environment, and files in cwd; agent_b touches academic papers, metadata, research questions, and configuration secrets. Both can read files and write files, so a shared workspace can expose sensitive material across the pair. The profiles do not document strong isolation or encryption, so leakage is plausible without extra controls.
conditions: IF both agents access the same directory tree, files from one can be read by the other.
IF either agent writes secrets or tokens into shared files, the other can read them.
mitigations: Store secrets outside the shared workspace.
Use per-agent directories with restrictive permissions.
Rotate any secrets that may have been written to disk.
requires-engineering: mount separate volumes per agent.
requires-engineering: add file-access allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can modify git state and write the filesystem; agent_b can also write the filesystem, though it cannot modify git state. Because agent_a's shared state is via filesystem and git only, concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace can corrupt files or create conflicting edits. The lack of documented locking or coordination makes the overlap dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or directory, file conflicts can occur.
IF agent_a commits while agent_b edits the same files, git history can diverge or be overwritten.
mitigations: Assign separate branches per agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes shared files.
Run git status before each commit.
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared paths.
requires-engineering: use a merge queue or transactional workspace.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can produce code or shell changes that agent_b may later consume in notebooks, prompts, or generated content. agent_b's content-writing workflow and API surfaces suggest it may act on upstream inputs, but no verification step is documented. This creates a plausible chain where errors from agent_a propagate into agent_b outputs, though direct autonomous action is not evidenced.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a-produced files or code as authoritative input, errors can cascade.
IF agent_a writes incorrect artifacts into shared files, agent_b may reproduce them in outputs.
mitigations: Require manual review of agent_a outputs before agent_b uses them.
Add a verification checklist for imported files.
Compare outputs against source data before publishing.
requires-engineering: add automated validation between agents.
requires-engineering: separate generation from execution stages.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles git credentials and API access in a terminal coding environment, while agent_b handles configuration secrets and academic-paper workflows in a local development environment. The profiles show different data classes and no shared retention or residency controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if regulated or sensitive data crosses the pair. The other agent is cited because the risk is about cross-agent handling.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace, both agents may process it under different handling assumptions.
IF retention or deletion requirements apply to files touched by both agents, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Document a single retention policy for both agents.
Review secret-handling paths before use.
requires-engineering: align logging and retention settings.
requires-engineering: add residency and DPA checks.
